title: Word List 7 — Test rehearsal
intro: Five parts, fifty points, laid out the way the real one is. Part III asks you to write the word yourself, and Part V asks for whole sentences — those are the two that catch people out.

parts.name: Part I
parts.title: Vocabulary Matching
parts.how: Choose the letter of the best definition for each word.
defs: always the same; not varying; boring
a sudden rush of animals or people, caused by fear
to do well; to be better or greater than others
able to survive under bad conditions; tough
of low to medium quality; barely passable
to bring or come into being
not planned; or suitable for everyday use
to use up, or to tire out
to add commas and periods to writing
not changing; or loyal and faithful

parts.name: Part II
parts.title: Multiple Choice: Meaning in Context
parts.how: Choose the word that best completes each sentence.

items.q: The thunderclap set off a ______ that carried the whole herd into the river.
items.why: A sudden rush caused by fear. A brawl is a fight; this was panic, not temper.

items.q: Two players who ______ on the ice are sent off for the rest of the game.
items.why: To fight noisily. The same word is the noun for the fight itself.

items.q: Sage is a ______ plant that can be left outside all winter.
items.why: Able to survive under bad conditions. Mediocre would mean it was simply a poor plant.

items.q: The meal was neither good nor bad, just ______ from the first course to the last.
items.why: Of low to medium quality, barely passable. Monotonous would mean every course tasted the same.

items.q: Making the same photocopy four hundred times is ______ work.
items.why: Always the same; not varying. The noun for the boredom it causes is monotony.

items.q: They came down off the mountain ______ and ate everything in the kitchen.
items.why: Very hungry. It can also mean eager for anything that satisfies a want.

items.q: A quiet voice will ______ a frightened animal faster than anything else will.
items.why: To make calm and relaxed. It also means to relieve soreness, as cold water does to a burn.

items.q: A morning of hauling bricks will ______ anybody who is not used to it.
items.why: To tire out. The same word means to use something up, and is the name for an engine's waste gases.

items.q: The custom of sending cards on that day did not ______ in this country at all.
items.why: To come into being. The noun is origin — the beginning of a thing.

items.q: He was an ordinary swimmer until he found the one stroke he could ______ at.
items.why: To do well; to be better than others.

parts.name: Part III
parts.title: Synonyms, Antonyms & Word Relationships
parts.how: Write the best vocabulary word on each line. Spelling counts.

items.q: An antonym for delicate or fragile:
items.why: Hardy — able to survive under bad conditions.

items.q: An antonym for excellent:
items.why: Mediocre — of low to medium quality, barely passable.

items.q: A synonym for very hungry:
items.why: Ravenous. It can also mean eager for whatever satisfies a want.

items.q: An antonym for varied or changing:
items.why: Monotonous (always the same) or constant (not changing). Either is defensible here.

items.q: A synonym for to calm or to comfort:
items.why: Soothe — to make calm and relaxed, or to make something hurt less.

items.q: A word meaning a person with much experience:
items.why: Veteran. It also means somebody who has served in the armed forces.

items.q: A word meaning to use something up completely:
items.why: Exhaust. The same word means to tire somebody out.

items.q: The noun that goes with the verb originate:
items.why: Origin — a beginning or coming into being.

items.q: The noun that goes with the verb punctuate:
items.why: Punctuation — the use of marks such as commas and periods.

items.q: The noun that goes with the adjective monotonous:
items.why: Monotony — lack of variety resulting in boredom.

parts.name: Part IV
parts.title: Parts of Speech
parts.how: Write noun, verb, adjective or adverb for the bold word as it is used.

items.q: Black smoke poured from the exhaust of the old truck.
items.why: A noun here — the thing the smoke came out of. Exhaust is usually a verb, which is why it is on the test.

items.q: The crowd began to stampede the moment somebody shouted.
items.why: A verb. Stampede is more often a noun, so look at what the word is doing in the sentence.

items.q: Two veteran players steadied the team when the match turned.
items.why: An adjective — it describes the players. On its own, veteran is a noun.

items.q: Sage is a hardy plant that survives the winter outdoors.
items.why: An adjective. It describes the plant.

items.q: The monotony of the long drive was broken by one good song.
items.why: A noun. Monotonous is the adjective; monotony is the thing itself.

parts.name: Part V
parts.title: Application & Critical Thinking
parts.how: Answer in complete sentences, using the vocabulary word correctly.

items.q: Explain the difference between a brawl and a stampede.
items.model: A brawl is a rough, noisy fight that people choose to start, but a stampede is a sudden rush of animals or people who are running because they are frightened.

items.q: Why would a chore feel monotonous? Use monotonous in your answer.
items.model: A chore feels monotonous when every part of it is exactly the same as the last, so there is nothing new to think about while you do it.

items.q: Use hardy and exhaust together in one logical sentence.
items.model: The hardy ponies could cross the moor all day without tiring, but the climb would exhaust an ordinary horse before noon.

items.q: Why might somebody be called a veteran without ever having been a soldier? Use veteran in your answer.
items.model: A veteran can also mean anybody with a great deal of experience at something, so a teacher of thirty years is a veteran of the classroom.

items.q: Explain what it means to be realistic about a plan. Use realistic in your answer.
items.model: Being realistic about a plan means seeing the thing as it actually is, so you allow enough time and money instead of hoping it all goes perfectly.
